analysis.one_liner: Extends federal gun background checks to ammunition purchases.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or vote and died when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require federally licensed sellers to run an instant background check through the existing national system before selling ammunition, and require private sellers to complete a check through a licensed dealer. It would also require dealers to keep sales records and report bulk ammunition purchases to law enforcement, ban Teflon-coated armor-piercing bullets and incendiary ammunition, and require a federal license to sell ammunition. It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans would benefit from a check that mirrors the one already required for gun purchases, which the bill cites as blocking more than 1.5 million unlawful sales over a decade. People prohibited from buying ammunition, and communities affected by mass shootings, would be the intended beneficiaries; law-abiding buyers would face a check that the bill says averages about 30 seconds.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Law-abiding buyers and communities hit by gun violence

how_it_helps.text: Licensed sellers must contact the existing instant background check system before transferring ammunition and verify the buyer's identity with photo ID, closing a gap in current law that requires checks for guns but not ammunition.

Checks on prohibited buyers can be refused, with records destroyed within three business days for lawful buyers; the bill cites more than 1.5 million blocked firearm sales over the last decade and says the check takes about 30 seconds on average.

Dealers must keep ammunition sales records and report bulk sales — a quantity set by the Justice Department as suggesting criminal intent — to state and local police, mirroring rules already used for guns to aid investigations.

analysis.who_pays: Licensed ammunition sellers face new licensing, recordkeeping, and reporting duties with fines up to $100,000 for knowing violations; buyers would show ID and undergo an instant check; private sellers would need to arrange transfers through licensed dealers. People barred from buying guns would be barred from buying ammunition.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ammunition dealers, private sellers, and prohibited buyers

drawbacks.text: The bill bans Teflon-coated and incendiary ammunition from future manufacture, sale, transfer, or possession, an expansion beyond closing background-check gaps that some would object to.

Ammunition is bought in far higher volume than firearms, with hundreds of thousands of transactions a day, so the background-check system would handle substantially higher traffic and costs Congress did not cap.
A rural exemption exists only where telecommunication is absent and officer coverage is extremely thin, so residents in low-density areas with phone service still face the new check process.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill applies an existing, fast system to ammunition with the stated aim of reducing gun violence, and exempts state permit holders, some remote areas, and existing owners of newly banned ammunition. The heavier burdens fall on dealers — licensing, recordkeeping, bulk-sale reporting, fines — and the volume of ammunition transactions would strain system capacity and raise enforcement costs. The benefit is intended to be fewer prohibited buyers obtaining ammunition; the cost is friction in a high-volume retail market.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in late March 2018, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it received no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Introduced on March 22, 2018, and referred the same day to the Senate Judiciary Committee, the bill saw no further action in the official record.
With three Democratic sponsors — Blumenthal, Murphy, and Whitehouse — and no Republican cosponsors, the bill had no path out of a committee chaired by the other party.
The 115th Congress ended January 3, 2019, and the bill was not reintroduced in the new Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No bill passed, so current law stands unchanged: ammunition sellers retain the lighter regulatory regime, and buyers prohibited from owning guns can still legally buy ammunition.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under Chairman Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill: no hearing, no markup, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors; the GOP-controlled Judiciary Committee took no action.

industries.note: Would need federal licenses, run background checks on every sale, keep records, and report bulk sales, facing fines up to $100,000 for knowing violations. Sales volume is high and margins thin, making compliance a real cost.
Bulk-sale and theft reports add investigative tools and workload; enforcing a new offense and civil fine structure adds prosecution work.
Dealers would collect a transfer fee for handling private-sale checks, a new revenue stream, while bearing new compliance costs.
